title: The Hymn of the Bell House
premise: When Noor Marchetti returns to his grandmother's decaying bell house to bury his twin brother Elias, he discovers the coffin holds a stranger — and that every photograph in the house now shows an extra chair where Elias used to sit. The house remembers a third sibling, one Noor's family spent seven years pretending never existed, and it wants him back. Guided by his grandmother's fragmented hymnal, Noor must learn the song's final verse without singing along, because those who sing it are absorbed into the house's chorus of the taken. In the end, Noor chooses truth over loyalty to his family's silence: he sings the verse aloud as an offering, trading his own place in the world for Elias's return — and walks out of the bell house as the extra chair.
about_author: Lior Delacroix is the pen name of a former church organist from coastal Louisiana who grew up in a house with more rooms than the blueprints allowed. Their fiction blends folk hymnody and domestic horror, and 'The Hymn of the Bell House' is their second novel.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. At the funeral home, Noor lifts the coffin lid and finds a stranger wearing Elias's face imperfectly, like a mask worn too long. He says nothing at the service, loyal to his mother's trembling insistence that grief makes people see things. Emotional beat: dread disguised as denial.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, moving into grandma's bell house to settle the estate. He catalogs every noise he's explained away since childhood — pipes, raccoons, settling wood — while unpacking boxes of photographs. Emotional beat: the fragile architecture of rationalization beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Comparing childhood photos to new prints he develops in the basement darkroom, he finds a wooden chair added beside him in every image, growing closer over the years until it touches his shoulder. Emotional beat: horror arriving quietly, through documentation rather than spectacle.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Hymnal
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In grandma's locked writing desk he finds a hand-bound hymnal with verses in no language he knows, the last page torn out. Marginalia warns: 'the fourth voice must not join.' Emotional beat: reluctant inheritance of a problem older than him.

chapters.title: What Mama Buried Twice
chapters.summary: Phone call chapter, mostly Mama's POV via voicemails she leaves at 3 a.m., slurring warnings about the house and begging Noor to burn the hymnal. She mentions 'the girl we gave them' before hanging up. Emotional beat: loyalty revealed as complicity.

chapters.title: The Bell House Sings Back
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Humming the hymnal's first verse absently, Noor hears the house answer in harmony — three voices where there should be none. The walls sweat cold. Emotional beat: the moment explanation dies and survival begins.

chapters.title: Neighbor with a Key
chapters.summary: Alternating Noor and Odile (elderly neighbor) POVs. Odile reveals her sister vanished into the house in 1968 and gives Noor her old key to the bell tower, warning that the song needs four voices and always has. Emotional beat: found family offered by a stranger who understands.

chapters.title: The Third Sibling
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, digging through county records and a shoebox of hospital bracelets. He learns of Colette Marchetti, born between the twins, institutionalized at six, dead on paper at nine — but the death certificate is signed in grandma's handwriting decades later. Emotional beat: the family's loyalty was a cover-up.

chapters.title: Chorus in the Walls
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The house escalates: furniture rearranges into a choir loft, the extra chair drags itself to the dinner table, and wet footprints of a child appear nightly. Noor stops sleeping. Emotional beat: siege mentality, isolation deepening.

chapters.title: Odile's Confession
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She admits she helped grandma lure Colette into the tower as children playing 'congregation,' believing the song was a game. Her guilt has kept her living next door for fifty years, listening. Emotional beat: shared sin, unexpected tenderness.

chapters.title: The Tower Key Turns
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Using Odile's key, Noor climbs the bell tower and finds the rope frayed into what looks like braided hair, and the great bell engraved with the hymn's melody. When he touches it, he hears Elias's voice among the chorus. Emotional beat: hope weaponized against him.

chapters.title: Elias Is Not Dead
chapters.summary: Elias's POV, disorienting and dreamlike. He wakes inside the house's memory, seated in the extra chair, watching Noor through photograph-paper eyes. He doesn't remember dying; he remembers being invited to sing. Emotional beat: the twist reframing everything — the wrong body wasn't a mistake.

chapters.title: The Trade They Made
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Piecing together grandma's letters, Noor learns the family traded Colette to the house seven years ago to save Elias from drowning — but the house took Elias anyway when the debt came due, sending back the stranger instead. Emotional beat: fury at the dead, grief curdling into resolve.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: Noor and Odile POVs alternating. Working from the bell's engraving, they reconstruct the hymn; each verse learned makes the house calmer, almost welcoming, which frightens Noor more than the screaming did. Emotional beat: seduction of belonging — the found family theme turned sinister.

chapters.title: Mama Comes Home
chapters.summary: Mama's POV. She arrives unannounced, sees the chair, and breaks: confessing she sang along once, at nineteen, and has been half-in ever since, which is why she left and why she drinks. She begs Noor to stop learning. Emotional beat: generational damage laid bare.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Following the child's footprints, Noor finds the torn final verse hidden inside the extra chair's hollow seat, written in Colette's hand — not a summoning but a release clause: the verse sung by a willing voice frees all previous singers. Emotional beat: revelation as liberation.

chapters.title: Odile Decides
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Understanding the verse requires a willing singer, Odile prepares to offer herself to reunite with her sister, and asks Noor to help her die meaningfully. Noor refuses to be her instrument. Emotional beat: love expressed as refusal.

chapters.title: The House Makes Its Offer
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The house manifests grandma's voice, offering a bargain: sing the verse and take Colette's place willingly, and Elias goes free. It shows him warm visions of the choir — belonging, rest, an end to explaining noises. Emotional beat: temptation at its most intimate.

chapters.title: Vespers
chapters.summary: All POVs converge. At dusk the house seals its doors, Mama trapped inside, Odile at the threshold with her key, Elias's presence pressing close. Noor takes his place in the choir loft beside the empty chair. Emotional beat: terrible calm before the climax.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, climax. Noor sings the final verse — but changes the ending line, offering himself not as a replacement for Colette but as a witness who names her, restoring her name and thereby voiding the original trade. The bell cracks. The house convulses, releasing its singers. Emotional beat: truth breaking loyalty's spell.

chapters.title: Four Voices, One Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, aftermath. Elias wakes gasping on the kitchen floor; Colette, freed after fifty years, is a fading child who thanks Noor and chooses to go. Mama and Odile embrace in the doorway. The house stands silent, ordinary, its photographs showing only the living. Emotional beat: grief and gratitude entwined.

chapters.title: Hymn Without a House
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, epilogue. A year later, Noor teaches the hymn's first three verses to a small found-family gathering — Mama sober, Odile visiting, Elias humming off-key — and keeps the final verse written down but unsung, a truth held ready rather than buried. Somewhere far away, a bell rings once. Emotional beat: hard-won peace, vigilance retained.
